extracted.intended_audience: linguists, humor researchers, and graduate students in semantics/pragmatics
extracted.subtask_description: Develop and apply a formal semantic framework that identifies the semantic properties and mechanisms (especially ambiguity) that make a text funny, and use that framework to distinguish jokes from non-jokes across categories such as sexual, ethnic, and political humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate ambiguity underlies verbal humor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Much of this book is about deliberate ambiguity... Deliberate ambiguity will be shown to underlie much, if not all, of verbal humor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity can be surface-level (simple enough to be perceived as deliberately ambiguous on the surface) or arise from deeper semantic analysis; identifying deliberately produced ambiguities is central to explaining why a text is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep semantic analysis as the core approach
rubrics_metrics.description: "Deep semantic analysis is the core of this approach to humor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method privileges rigorous, formal semantic examination of texts (not merely pragmatic or sociological accounts) to reveal hidden or structural ambiguities and relations that generate humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate necessary and sufficient semantic conditions for funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The goal of the theory is to formulate the necessary and sufficient conditions, in purely semantic terms, for a text to be funny."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to produce precise, testable semantic criteria such that possession of the specified semantic properties entails that a text is a joke (and absence entails non-joke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of jokes by semantic property sets
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a formal semantic analysis of a text yields a certain set of semantic properties which the text possesses, then the text is recognized as a joke."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies a rule-like mapping from identified semantic properties to the classification 'joke'; analyses should enumerate the semantic properties used for recognition and show how they combine to produce funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match formal theory to native-speaker intuitive ability
rubrics_metrics.description: "As any modern linguistic theory, this semantic theory of humor attempts to match a natural intuitive ability which the native speaker has... to distinguish a joke from a non-joke."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory should account for common-sense judgments about humor by speakers — i.e., it must predict when speakers will intuitively perceive text as funny, aligning formal criteria with empirical intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of modern linguistic theory to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: "The book is the first ever application of modern linguistic theory to the study of humor and it puts forward a formal semantic theory of verbal humor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should employ and adapt techniques from contemporary linguistics/semantics rather than relying solely on folk or ad hoc descriptions; theoretical rigor and formalization are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization and coverage of humor types
rubrics_metrics.description: Table of contents indicates focused chapters on categories: "Semantic Theory of Humor", "Sexual Humor", "Ethnic Humor", "Political Humor" (plus general survey and theory chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework is intended to be applied across multiple humor domains; evaluations should consider how the proposed semantic mechanisms operate in different topical genres (sexual, ethnic, political) and whether the criteria generalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and scanned/textual material (access/format note)
rubrics_metrics.description: PDF accessibility summary notes the material is based on scanned pages and may not be fully accessible; content likely supports searchable/ selectable text based on OCR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers/analysts should be aware that some examples or illustrations in the scanned text may not be screen-reader-friendly; when extracting data/examples, verify OCR accuracy and consult original if possible.
